stem:
An obstetric registrar reviews a woman at 12 weeks, admitted after three weeks of persistent vomiting with very little food intake; she has lost 7% of her body weight. Saline and potassium replacement are running. 

| Observation | Result |
|---|---|
| Sodium | 138 mmol/L |
| Potassium | 3.6 mmol/L |
| Glucose | 4.7 mmol/L |

She is alert, with no confusion, ataxia or eye signs, and still cannot keep oral medicines down. The team plans to add dextrose-containing fluid.

Which additional treatment plan is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: IV pyridoxine before the dextrose infusion begins
options.explanation: Pyridoxine may help nausea, but it does not prevent the thiamine-deficiency encephalopathy that carbohydrate loading can precipitate.

options.label: B
options.text: IV thiamine before the dextrose infusion begins
options.explanation: After prolonged vomiting and poor intake, give parenteral thiamine before dextrose, because glucose metabolism consumes thiamine and can precipitate Wernicke’s encephalopathy.

options.label: C
options.text: Oral thiamine once she can keep tablets down
options.explanation: She cannot absorb oral medicines reliably and dextrose is about to be given, so oral thiamine would come too late.

options.label: D
options.text: IV thiamine only if confusion, ataxia or nystagmus develops
options.explanation: Wernicke’s encephalopathy should be prevented, not awaited; neurological signs mean damage has begun.

options.label: E
options.text: IV thiamine once the dextrose infusion is established
options.explanation: Giving dextrose first can precipitate Wernicke’s encephalopathy in a thiamine-depleted patient; the order matters.

context: Give thiamine before planned carbohydrate administration after prolonged vomiting and poor intake.
